title: Population Health, Evidence and Professional Practice

notes.h: Epidemiological study designs: choosing and critiquing them
notes.body:
Epidemiology asks who gets disease, where, when and why. Designs are descriptive (case series, cross-sectional surveys, ecological studies) or analytical (case-control, cohort, intervention). The central question is always how well a design separates a real association from chance, bias and confounding.

- Ecological study: compares groups or areas, not individuals. It is cheap and generates hypotheses, but risks the ecological fallacy (assuming a group-level link holds for individuals).
- Cross-sectional study: measures exposure and outcome at one time point. It gives prevalence but usually cannot establish temporality.
- Case-control study: samples by outcome (cases versus controls) and compares past exposures. It is efficient for rare diseases and long latency and gives an odds ratio. It is prone to recall bias and to selection bias in choosing controls. Classic example: Doll and Hill's 1950 smoking and lung cancer study.
- Cohort study: samples by exposure and follows people forward (or uses historical records). It shows temporality and gives incidence and relative risk for several outcomes. It is slow and costly, and loss to follow-up biases results. Examples: the British Doctors Study (from 1951) and Framingham (from 1948).
- Randomised controlled trial (RCT): randomisation balances known and unknown confounders. Allocation concealment, blinding and intention-to-treat analysis limit bias. Reporting follows CONSORT.
- Systematic review and meta-analysis: pools studies found by a reproducible search (PRISMA 2020). The result is only as good as the included studies, and publication bias can distort it.

Bias is systematic error: selection bias (who gets in) or information bias (how data are measured, including recall and observer bias). Confounding occurs when a third factor is associated with the exposure, independently affects the outcome and is not on the causal pathway; smoking confounds an apparent alcohol–lung cancer link. Control it by randomisation, restriction, matching, stratification or multivariable adjustment.

Bradford Hill (1965) proposed viewpoints for judging causation: strength, consistency, specificity, temporality, biological gradient, plausibility, coherence, experiment and analogy. Only temporality is essential.

Worked illustration: testing whether a rare childhood cancer is linked to living near power lines would need a cohort of millions. A case-control study using registry cases and matched population controls is feasible.

Exam pitfalls:
- Calling a case-control study a 'retrospective cohort'. Ask whether sampling was by outcome or by exposure.
- Claiming RCTs remove all bias. Poor blinding or attrition can still bias results.
- Treating an adjusted association as proof of causation. Residual confounding remains.

notes.h: Measures of disease frequency and association
notes.body:
Frequency:
- Prevalence = existing cases ÷ population, at a point or over a period. Useful for planning services.
- Incidence proportion (risk) = new cases over a period ÷ population at risk at the start.
- Incidence rate = new cases ÷ person-time at risk (24 cases in 4,000 person-years = 6 per 1,000 person-years).
- In a steady state with low prevalence, prevalence ≈ incidence rate × mean duration. Treatment that prolongs life without cure, such as antiretroviral therapy for HIV, raises prevalence.
- Age standardisation. Direct standardisation applies age-specific rates to a standard population. Indirect standardisation gives the standardised mortality ratio (SMR = observed ÷ expected deaths × 100).

Association, from a 2×2 table where a and b are exposed (cases, non-cases) and c and d are unexposed:
- Relative risk (RR) = [a/(a+b)] ÷ [c/(c+d)]. Used in cohorts and RCTs.
- Odds ratio (OR) = ad/bc. Used in case-control studies. It approximates the RR when the outcome is rare.
- Risk difference (attributable risk) = risk in exposed − risk in unexposed.
- Attributable fraction in the exposed = (RR − 1)/RR.
- Population attributable fraction (PAF) = Pe(RR − 1)/[1 + Pe(RR − 1)], where Pe is the proportion exposed.

Trial measures:
- Absolute risk reduction (ARR) = control event rate − experimental event rate.
- Relative risk reduction (RRR) = ARR ÷ control event rate.
- Number needed to treat (NNT) = 1/ARR, rounded up. The same calculation for harms gives the number needed to harm (NNH).

Worked example: 1,000 smokers have 30 cases; 2,000 non-smokers have 20.
- Risks are 3% and 1%, so RR = 3.
- Risk difference = 2 percentage points, so NNH = 50.
- Attributable fraction in smokers = 2/3 = 67%.
- Pe = 1/3, so PAF = (2/3)/(5/3) = 0.4. Check: overall risk is 50/3,000 = 1.67%, and (1.67 − 1)/1.67 = 0.4.

An RR or OR of 1 means no association. A 95% confidence interval that includes 1 is compatible with no effect at the 5% level.

Exam pitfalls:
- Quoting relative effects alone. An RRR of 50% can be an ARR of 0.1% when baseline risk is low.
- Calculating an RR from a case-control study. The investigator fixes the number of cases, so risks cannot be estimated.
- Forgetting to round the NNT up.
- Confusing incidence with prevalence when survival changes.

notes.h: Screening: principles, test performance and pitfalls
notes.body:
Screening is the systematic offer of a test to people without symptoms, to identify those at higher risk so that further tests or treatment can reduce harm. It differs from case-finding (opportunistic) and from diagnosis (testing people with symptoms).

Wilson and Jungner (WHO, 1968) set the classic criteria:
- an important health problem with known natural history and a recognisable early stage
- a suitable, acceptable test
- effective treatment that works better early, with facilities and an agreed policy on whom to treat
- costs balanced against overall spending, and case-finding as a continuing process.

The UK National Screening Committee (UK NSC) advises ministers. Its criteria stress RCT evidence that screening reduces mortality or morbidity, and that benefit outweighs harm.

NHS programmes in England include bowel (FIT), breast (mammography), cervical (HPV primary testing), abdominal aortic aneurysm (ultrasound for men in the year they turn 65), diabetic eye, and antenatal and newborn screening. Targeted lung cancer screening is being rolled out. There is no population PSA screening programme: in May 2026 the UK NSC recommended against screening all men (or Black men as a group) and recommended only targeted two-yearly PSA screening for men aged 45–61 with a BRCA2 variant and a relevant family history, which England plans to introduce from 2027.

Test performance:
- Sensitivity = TP/(TP + FN). Specificity = TN/(TN + FP). Both are properties of the test.
- Positive predictive value (PPV) = TP/(TP + FP). Negative predictive value (NPV) = TN/(TN + FN). Both vary with prevalence.
- Likelihood ratio (LR) positive = sensitivity/(1 − specificity). LR negative = (1 − sensitivity)/specificity.

Worked example: screen 10,000 people, with prevalence 1%, sensitivity 90% and specificity 95%.
- 100 are diseased: TP 90, FN 10.
- 9,900 are not: TN 9,405, FP 495.
- PPV = 90/585 = 15.4%; NPV = 99.9%. Most positive results are false alarms.

Biases that flatter screening:
- Lead-time bias: earlier diagnosis lengthens survival from diagnosis without delaying death.
- Length-time bias: slow-growing disease is over-detected.
- Overdiagnosis: detecting disease that would never cause harm.
- Healthy volunteer bias: people who attend are healthier.
Mortality in an RCT, not survival from diagnosis, is therefore the proper outcome. The Independent UK Panel on Breast Cancer Screening (2012) judged that breast screening reduces mortality, but that roughly three women are overdiagnosed for every death prevented.

Exam pitfalls:
- Assuming a sensitive test has a high PPV.
- Ignoring harms: anxiety, false reassurance, invasive follow-up and overtreatment.
- Forgetting that informed choice, not maximum uptake, is the aim of UK screening.

notes.h: Statistics for medicine: inference, tests and interpretation
notes.body:
Data types decide the summary and the test. Data may be categorical (nominal or ordinal) or numerical (discrete or continuous). Summarise normal data by mean and standard deviation (SD), and skewed data by median and interquartile range.

Precision:
- Standard error of the mean (SE) = SD/√n.
- 95% confidence interval (CI) ≈ mean ± 1.96 × SE. Example: mean systolic BP 140 mmHg, SD 12, n = 36. SE = 2, so the 95% CI is 136.1 to 143.9 mmHg.
- In a normal distribution about 68% of values lie within 1 SD of the mean, and 95% within 1.96 SD.

Hypothesis testing:
- The p-value is the probability of a result at least this extreme if the null hypothesis (H₀) were true. It is not the probability that H₀ is true.
- Type I error (α) is a false positive, conventionally 0.05. Type II error (β) is a false negative. Power = 1 − β, typically 80–90%.
- Power rises with sample size, effect size and α, and falls with variability.
- Multiple testing inflates type I error. Bonferroni correction divides α by the number of tests.

Choosing a test:
- Two independent means (normal data): unpaired t-test. Paired data: paired t-test. More than two groups: ANOVA.
- Non-parametric equivalents: Mann–Whitney U, Wilcoxon signed-rank, Kruskal–Wallis.
- Proportions: chi-squared test, or Fisher's exact test when expected counts are small.
- Two continuous variables: Pearson r, or Spearman's rank for non-normal data.
- Regression: linear for continuous outcomes; logistic for binary outcomes (adjusted ORs); Cox proportional hazards for time-to-event data (hazard ratios), with Kaplan–Meier curves and the log-rank test.

Trial analysis:
- Intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis keeps participants in their randomised arms and preserves randomisation. Per-protocol analysis can exaggerate benefit.
- Statistical significance is not clinical importance.
- Subgroup analyses should be pre-specified and tested for interaction. Otherwise treat them as hypothesis-generating.

Exam pitfalls:
- Confusing SD (spread of the data) with SE (precision of the estimate).
- Reading p = 0.06 as proof of no effect. Look at the confidence interval.
- Using t-tests on skewed data or on proportions.
- Treating correlation as causation, or r as a slope.

notes.h: Health inequalities: patterns, explanations and responses
notes.body:
Health inequalities are systematic, avoidable and unfair differences in health between groups, for example by deprivation, ethnicity, sex, geography or inclusion-health status (such as homelessness or imprisonment). The social gradient means health worsens step by step down the social ladder, not only at the bottom. The Whitehall studies of civil servants, with Michael Marmot leading Whitehall II from 1985, showed mortality and coronary disease rising with lower employment grade, only partly explained by smoking and other risk factors.

Key reports:
- Black Report (1980) offered four explanations: artefact; natural or social selection (ill people drift down); cultural or behavioural; and materialist or structural (income, housing, work). It favoured the materialist explanation.
- Acheson Inquiry (1998): recommended cross-government action, prioritising families with children.
- Marmot Review, 'Fair Society, Healthy Lives' (2010), set six objectives: give every child the best start; maximise capabilities and control; fair employment and good work; a healthy standard of living; healthy and sustainable places; and stronger ill-health prevention. It introduced proportionate universalism: universal action scaled in intensity to need. 'The Marmot Review 10 Years On' (2020) found that improvement in life expectancy had stalled and inequalities had widened.

Frameworks:
- Dahlgren and Whitehead's rainbow model (1991): individual factors sit inside layers of lifestyle, social networks, living and working conditions, and wider socioeconomic conditions.
- Julian Tudor Hart's inverse care law (1971): good care varies inversely with need.
- Wilkinson and Pickett (The Spirit Level, 2009) argue that more unequal societies fare worse overall. This is contested.

Policy and law:
- The Equality Act 2010 sets out nine protected characteristics and a public sector equality duty.
- NHS bodies have statutory duties to have regard to reducing health inequalities (Health and Social Care Act 2012, as amended by the Health and Care Act 2022, which made integrated care systems statutory).
- NHS England's Core20PLUS5 targets the most deprived 20% by the Index of Multiple Deprivation, plus locally chosen groups, across five clinical areas.

Applied illustration: a practice in a deprived area has poor hypertension control. A proportionate-universalist response keeps universal checks and adds outreach clinics, interpreters and flexible appointments for the worst-served groups.

Exam pitfalls:
- Equating inequality (any difference) with inequity (unfair, avoidable difference).
- Blaming behaviour alone. Behaviours are socially patterned (the 'causes of the causes').
- Forgetting that interventions relying on individual agency can widen gaps (intervention-generated inequality).

notes.h: Medical ethics: frameworks and core debates
notes.body:
Ethics supplies the reasons for clinical choices. Law sets the minimum, and GMC guidance sets professional standards. Good answers name the tension, apply more than one framework and reach a defended conclusion.

Frameworks:
- Four principles (Beauchamp and Childress, 1979 onwards): respect for autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice. They are prima facie and must be weighed against each other. Gillon added attention to scope (to whom we owe them).
- Consequentialism (Bentham, Mill): maximise overall good. Act utilitarianism judges each act; rule utilitarianism follows generally beneficial rules. The main criticism is that it can sacrifice individuals.
- Deontology (Kant): duties bind regardless of outcome. Never treat people merely as a means. This grounds consent and truth-telling.
- Virtue ethics (Aristotle): what would a practically wise, good doctor do? Care ethics and casuistry stress relationships and paradigm cases.

Core debates:
- Autonomy versus beneficence. A capacitous adult may refuse life-saving treatment (Re T 1992; Re B 2002). Paternalism needs justification, usually lack of capacity.
- Truth-telling. Withholding information is rarely justified; Montgomery (2015) keeps the therapeutic exception narrow.
- Double effect. An act with a foreseen bad effect may be permissible if the act is good or neutral, only the good is intended, the bad effect is not the means, and there is proportionate reason. It is used for symptom relief at the end of life. Withdrawing futile treatment was treated as an omission in Airedale NHS Trust v Bland (1993).
- End of life. Euthanasia is murder, and assisting suicide is an offence under s2 Suicide Act 1961. The courts left reform to Parliament (R (Nicklinson) v Ministry of Justice 2014). The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill passed the Commons in 2025 but fell at Lords committee stage in spring 2026; a new private member's bill was introduced in June 2026, so check its current status.
- Justice. QALYs underpin NICE cost-effectiveness. Critics cite ageism and disability bias, and the 'rule of rescue' favours identifiable lives. Daniels and Sabin's 'accountability for reasonableness' demands decisions that are public, relevant, revisable and enforced. See R v Cambridge HA, ex p B (1995).
- Conscientious objection. Section 4 Abortion Act 1967 covers only hands-on participation (Greater Glasgow Health Board v Doogan 2014). Patients must still be able to access care.

Worked illustration: a man refuses to let you tell his wife he has HIV. Confidentiality and autonomy conflict with non-maleficence towards an identifiable person at risk. Try persuasion first. GMC guidance permits disclosure as a last resort to protect her from serious harm.

Exam pitfalls:
- Listing principles without weighing them.
- Conflating legal with ethical.
- Treating 'best interests' as the doctor's personal opinion.

Consent needs capacity, information and voluntariness. Touching without consent to the procedure's broad nature is battery (Chatterton v Gerson 1981); inadequate risk disclosure is negligence.
- Montgomery v Lanarkshire HB [2015] UKSC 11: doctors must take reasonable care to ensure patients know of material risks and reasonable alternatives. A risk is material if a reasonable person in the patient's position would attach significance to it, or if the doctor knows (or should know) that this patient would.
- McCulloch v Forth Valley HB [2023] UKSC 26: which alternatives are 'reasonable' is a matter of professional judgement (Bolam, subject to Bolitho).
- Capacitous adults may refuse any treatment (Re T 1992; Re B 2002), even in pregnancy (St George's v S 1998).

Capacity: the Mental Capacity Act 2005 (MCA) applies from age 16.
- Principles (s1): presume capacity; take all practicable steps to support the decision; an unwise decision is not incapacity; act in best interests; prefer the less restrictive option.
- The test is decision- and time-specific. After A Local Authority v JB [2021] UKSC 52, ask first whether the person can understand, retain, use or weigh, and communicate (s3), then whether any inability is caused by an impairment or disturbance of the mind or brain (s2).
- Best interests (s4) weighs past and present wishes, beliefs and values, and carers' views, seen from the patient's perspective (Aintree v James [2013] UKSC 67).
- A health and welfare LPA or a valid, applicable advance decision (ss24–26) binds clinicians (makers must be 18+). Refusing life-sustaining treatment requires writing, signature, witness and an express 'even if life is at risk' statement.
- An IMCA is needed for serious medical treatment if no one is appropriate to consult. The Court of Protection resolves disputes.
- Deprivation of liberty in a hospital or care home needs DoLS authorisation (elsewhere, a Court of Protection order) (acid test: Cheshire West [2014] UKSC 19); the Liberty Protection Safeguards have not been implemented.

Children: 16–17-year-olds consent under s8 Family Law Reform Act 1969; under-16s if Gillick competent (1986), with the Fraser guidelines for contraception. Courts have overridden minors' refusals of life-saving treatment (Re W 1992).

Confidentiality is a common law, data protection (UK GDPR, DPA 2018) and professional duty (GMC 2017). Disclosure is permitted:
- with consent
- when required by law (notifiable diseases; FGM in under-18s)
- in the public interest to prevent serious harm (W v Egdell 1990).
ABC v St George's [2020] EWHC 455 (QB) recognised a duty in some cases to balance an at-risk third party's interests. For driving, the legal duty to notify the DVLA rests with the driver. Persuade first; if the patient keeps driving, tell them, then inform the DVLA.

Exam pitfalls:
- Applying the diagnostic test first.
- Citing Bolam for disclosure.
- Believing next of kin can consent for adults.

Good Medical Practice (GMC, 2024 edition, in force from 30 January 2024) has four domains: knowledge, skills and development; patients, partnership and communication; colleagues, culture and safety; and trust and professionalism. The 2024 edition strengthened duties on compassionate and inclusive workplaces, and on challenging bullying, discrimination and sexual harassment. Medical students are held to equivalent standards.

Consultation skills:
- Calgary–Cambridge guide: initiating, gathering information, physical examination, explanation and planning, closing. Structure and relationship-building run throughout.
- Ideas, concerns and expectations (ICE), open-to-closed questioning, summarising and signposting.
- Shared decision-making: present options, including doing nothing, using absolute numbers and natural frequencies. Use 'chunk and check' and teach-back.
- Use professional interpreters, not family, and never children.

Breaking bad news with SPIKES (Baile and colleagues, 2000):
- Setting
- Perception (what does the patient know?)
- Invitation (how much do they want to know?)
- Knowledge (warning shot, then small, jargon-free chunks)
- Emotions (empathy and silence)
- Strategy and summary.

Candour:
- Statutory duty of candour: Regulation 20 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014 requires registered organisations to notify, apologise and give information after notifiable safety incidents.
- Professional duty: each doctor must be open, apologise and explain when things go wrong (GMC/NMC openness and honesty guidance). An apology is not an admission of liability (s2 Compensation Act 2006).
- Report incidents for learning. The GMC has said it will not ask doctors for reflective notes in fitness to practise cases.

Raising concerns: act when patient safety is at risk from a colleague's conduct, health or performance, or from systems. Escalate through supervisor, clinical director, medical director and then the regulator. The Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 protects whistleblowers. Freedom to Speak Up Guardians followed the Francis reports (Mid Staffordshire Inquiry 2013; Freedom to Speak Up 2015).

Accountability:
- Medical Practitioners Tribunal Service tribunals decide fitness to practise.
- Gross negligence manslaughter requires duty, breach, causation of death and conduct so bad as to be criminal (R v Adomako 1995).
- In the Bawa-Garba case, the High Court ordered erasure at the GMC's request. The Court of Appeal reinstated the tribunal's suspension (Bawa-Garba v GMC [2018] EWCA Civ 1879), prompting reviews of systemic pressures and reflection.

Applied illustration: an FY1 smells alcohol on a registrar about to operate. Patient safety comes first. Stop the registrar operating, escalate at once to the consultant, then support the colleague's health.

Exam pitfalls:
- Treating professionalism as etiquette rather than accountability.
- Confusing statutory (organisational) and professional (individual) candour.
- Failing to escalate because the colleague is senior.

cards.f: What defines a case-control study?
cards.b: Participants are selected according to whether they have the outcome (cases) or not (controls). Their past exposures are then compared, usually giving an odds ratio.

cards.f: What defines a cohort study?
cards.b: Participants are selected by exposure status and followed over time (prospectively or using historical records) to compare how often the outcome occurs. It gives incidence and relative risk.

cards.f: What is the ecological fallacy?
cards.b: Wrongly inferring that an association seen between groups or areas also holds for individuals within those groups.

cards.f: Why is a case-control design preferred for rare diseases?
cards.b: Cases can be sampled directly (e.g. from a registry), so you do not need to follow a huge population to accumulate enough outcomes.

cards.f: Define confounding.
cards.b: Distortion of an exposure–outcome association by a third factor that is associated with the exposure, independently affects the outcome, and is not on the causal pathway.

cards.f: Name four ways of controlling confounding.
cards.b: At the design stage: randomisation, restriction and matching. At analysis: stratification and multivariable adjustment (e.g. regression).

cards.f: What is recall bias and which design is most prone to it?
cards.b: Systematic difference in how accurately cases and controls remember past exposures, because cases search harder for explanations. It is classically a problem in case-control studies.

cards.f: Which Bradford Hill viewpoint is essential for causation?
cards.b: Temporality: the exposure must come before the outcome. The others (strength, consistency, gradient, plausibility and so on) support causation without being required.

cards.f: What does allocation concealment protect against in an RCT?
cards.b: Selection bias at enrolment. Recruiters cannot know or influence the next allocation. It is different from blinding, which protects against performance and detection bias after allocation.

cards.f: Why can a cross-sectional study rarely establish causation?
cards.b: Exposure and outcome are measured at the same time, so it is usually impossible to know which came first (reverse causation). Prevalent cases also over-represent long-lasting disease.

cards.f: Prevalence vs incidence?
cards.b: Prevalence is the proportion of a population with the disease at a point or over a period (existing cases). Incidence counts new cases arising in a population at risk over time.

cards.f: How are prevalence, incidence and duration related?
cards.b: In a steady state with low prevalence, prevalence ≈ incidence rate × mean duration. So treatments that prolong life without cure increase prevalence.

cards.f: Formula for the relative risk from a 2×2 table (a, b exposed; c, d unexposed; a, c cases).
cards.b: RR = [a/(a+b)] ÷ [c/(c+d)], the risk in the exposed divided by the risk in the unexposed.

cards.f: Formula for the odds ratio.
cards.b: OR = (a × d)/(b × c), the cross-product ratio. It approximates the relative risk when the outcome is rare.

cards.f: Control event rate 20%, treatment event rate 15%: give the ARR, RRR and NNT.
cards.b: ARR = 5 percentage points; RRR = 5/20 = 25%; NNT = 1/0.05 = 20.

cards.f: Define the population attributable fraction (PAF).
cards.b: The proportion of all cases in a population that would be prevented if the exposure were removed (assuming causality). PAF = Pe(RR − 1)/[1 + Pe(RR − 1)].

cards.f: Attributable fraction in the exposed when RR = 4?
cards.b: (RR − 1)/RR = 3/4 = 75% of cases among exposed people are attributable to the exposure (if causal).

cards.f: What is a standardised mortality ratio (SMR)?
cards.b: Observed deaths ÷ deaths expected if the study population had the age-specific rates of a standard population, × 100. It comes from indirect standardisation; an SMR above 100 means excess mortality.

cards.f: Why can't a relative risk be calculated from a case-control study?
cards.b: The researcher fixes the ratio of cases to controls, so the proportion with disease in each exposure group does not reflect true risk. Only the odds ratio is valid.

cards.f: An incidence rate of 24 cases in 4,000 person-years is?
cards.b: 24/4,000 = 0.006 per person-year, or 6 per 1,000 person-years.

cards.f: Define screening.
cards.b: The systematic offer of testing to people who have no symptoms of a condition, to identify those at higher risk so that further tests or treatment can reduce harm.

cards.f: Who wrote the classic screening criteria and when?
cards.b: Wilson and Jungner, for the World Health Organization, in 1968.

cards.f: Which body advises UK ministers on screening programmes?
cards.b: The UK National Screening Committee (UK NSC). It assesses evidence against its criteria, including RCT evidence of benefit outweighing harm.

cards.f: Sensitivity vs specificity?
cards.b: Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the disease who test positive, TP/(TP+FN). Specificity is the proportion of people without the disease who test negative, TN/(TN+FP).

cards.f: Why does PPV fall when prevalence falls?
cards.b: With fewer true cases, the false positives from the large disease-free group make up a bigger share of all positive results, even though sensitivity and specificity are unchanged.

cards.f: Define lead-time bias.
cards.b: An apparent improvement in survival because screening brings diagnosis forward in time, while the time of death is unchanged.

cards.f: Define length-time bias.
cards.b: Screening preferentially detects slow-growing, less aggressive disease because it spends longer in the detectable pre-clinical phase. Screen-detected cases therefore look as though they have a better prognosis.

cards.f: What is overdiagnosis?
cards.b: Detection of a condition that would never have caused symptoms or death in the person's lifetime. It leads to unnecessary treatment and is a key harm of breast and prostate screening.

cards.f: Sensitivity 90%, specificity 95%: calculate LR+ and LR−.
Why is disease-specific mortality in an RCT the preferred outcome for evaluating screening?
cards.b: Survival from diagnosis is inflated by lead-time, length-time and overdiagnosis bias. Randomising whole populations and comparing deaths avoids these biases.

cards.f: Standard deviation vs standard error?
cards.b: The SD describes the spread of individual values in the sample. The SE (= SD/√n) describes the precision of the sample mean as an estimate of the population mean.

cards.f: Mean 140, SD 12, n = 36: what is the 95% CI?
Define a p-value.
cards.b: The probability of obtaining a result at least as extreme as the one observed if the null hypothesis were true. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

cards.f: Type I vs type II error?
cards.b: Type I (α) is rejecting a true null hypothesis (a false positive). Type II (β) is failing to reject a false null hypothesis (a false negative).

cards.f: What is statistical power, and what increases it?
cards.b: Power = 1 − β, the probability of detecting a true effect of a given size. It increases with larger sample size, larger effect size, higher α and lower variability.

cards.f: Which test compares two independent proportions?
cards.b: The chi-squared test, or Fisher's exact test when expected cell counts are small.

cards.f: Non-parametric alternative to the unpaired t-test?
cards.b: The Mann–Whitney U test (Wilcoxon rank-sum). For paired data use the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

cards.f: What is intention-to-treat analysis and why use it?
cards.b: Analysing participants in the groups to which they were randomised, whatever treatment they actually received. It preserves the balance created by randomisation and reflects real-world effectiveness.

cards.f: What does a hazard ratio of 0.7 from Cox regression mean?
cards.b: At any point during follow-up, the instantaneous event rate in the intervention group is 30% lower than in the comparator (assuming proportional hazards).

cards.f: What is the multiple comparisons problem?
cards.b: Each extra test adds a chance of a false positive. With 20 independent tests at α = 0.05, about one 'significant' result is expected by chance alone. Bonferroni correction divides α by the number of tests.

cards.f: Define health inequalities.
cards.b: Systematic, avoidable and unfair differences in health between population groups, e.g. by deprivation, ethnicity, sex or geography.

cards.f: What is the social gradient in health?
cards.b: Health outcomes worsen step by step with each step down the socioeconomic ladder, not just among the poorest. It was shown in the Whitehall studies of civil servants.

cards.f: Name the four explanations for inequalities in the Black Report (1980).
cards.b: Artefact, natural or social selection, cultural or behavioural, and materialist or structural. The report favoured materialist explanations.

cards.f: What is the inverse care law?
cards.b: Julian Tudor Hart (1971): the availability of good medical care tends to vary inversely with the need for it in the population served.

cards.f: What is proportionate universalism?
cards.b: From the Marmot Review (2010): actions should be universal but with a scale and intensity proportionate to the level of disadvantage.

cards.f: List the layers of the Dahlgren and Whitehead (1991) model.
cards.b: From the centre outwards: age, sex and constitutional factors; individual lifestyle; social and community networks; living and working conditions; general socioeconomic, cultural and environmental conditions.

cards.f: What did 'The Marmot Review 10 Years On' (2020) find?
cards.b: Improvement in life expectancy in England had stalled, health inequalities had widened, and life expectancy had fallen for women in the most deprived areas.

cards.f: What is Core20PLUS5?
cards.b: An NHS England approach to reducing healthcare inequalities. It focuses on the most deprived 20% of the national population (by IMD) plus locally defined groups, across five clinical priority areas.

cards.f: Inequality vs inequity?
cards.b: Inequality is any measurable difference in health. Inequity is a difference judged unfair and avoidable, which carries a moral claim for action.

cards.f: What is intervention-generated inequality?
cards.b: When an intervention benefits advantaged groups more than disadvantaged ones, widening the gap. This is a risk with information campaigns that rely on individual resources.

cards.f: State the four principles of Beauchamp and Childress.
cards.b: Respect for autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice. They are prima facie duties to be weighed against each other.

cards.f: Act vs rule utilitarianism?
cards.b: Act utilitarianism judges each action by its consequences. Rule utilitarianism follows the rules whose general observance produces the best consequences (e.g. keeping confidences).

cards.f: Kant's humanity formulation?
cards.b: Act so that you treat humanity, in yourself or others, always as an end and never merely as a means. It grounds informed consent and truth-telling.

cards.f: Conditions of the doctrine of double effect.
cards.b: The act is good or neutral in itself; only the good effect is intended; the bad effect is not the means to the good; there is proportionate reason for accepting the bad effect.

cards.f: What did Airedale NHS Trust v Bland (1993) decide?
cards.b: Withdrawing artificial nutrition and hydration from a patient in a persistent vegetative state could be lawful as an omission in his best interests, where continuing treatment conferred no benefit.

cards.f: What did R (Nicklinson) v Ministry of Justice (2014) decide?
cards.b: The Supreme Court declined to declare s2 Suicide Act 1961 incompatible with Article 8 ECHR, holding that Parliament was the proper forum to consider changing the law on assisted suicide at that time.

cards.f: What is a QALY?
cards.b: A quality-adjusted life year combines length and quality of life: one year in perfect health = 1 QALY. NICE uses cost per QALY to judge cost-effectiveness.

cards.f: What are Daniels and Sabin's conditions of 'accountability for reasonableness'?
cards.b: Publicity, relevance, revisability (appeals) and enforcement (regulation), for fair priority-setting under reasonable disagreement.

cards.f: What is the 'rule of rescue'?
cards.b: The strong impulse to save identifiable individuals in immediate danger regardless of cost. It can conflict with cost-effective allocation for 'statistical' lives.

cards.f: What did Greater Glasgow Health Board v Doogan (2014) decide?
cards.b: The conscientious objection right in s4 Abortion Act 1967 covers only actual 'hands-on' participation in treatment, not supervisory or administrative tasks.

cards.f: What are the three elements of valid consent?
cards.b: Capacity, sufficient information, and voluntariness (freedom from coercion or undue influence).

cards.f: State the Montgomery (2015) materiality test.
cards.b: A risk is material if a reasonable person in the patient's position would be likely to attach significance to it, or if the doctor knows or should reasonably know that this particular patient would.

cards.f: What did McCulloch v Forth Valley HB (2023) add to Montgomery?
cards.b: Which treatment options count as 'reasonable alternatives' to discuss is decided by professional judgement under the Bolam test (subject to Bolitho). The duty to disclose material risks of those options remains.

cards.f: State the MCA 2005 s1 principles.
cards.b: Presume capacity; take all practicable steps to support decision-making; an unwise decision is not proof of incapacity; act in best interests; consider the less restrictive option.

cards.f: What are the four functional abilities in s3 MCA 2005?
cards.b: To understand the relevant information, retain it, use or weigh it as part of deciding, and communicate the decision by any means.

cards.f: What did A Local Authority v JB (2021) say about the order of the capacity test?
cards.b: Ask first whether the person can make the decision (the functional test in s3), then whether any inability is caused by an impairment or disturbance of the mind or brain (s2).

cards.f: Formal requirements of an advance decision refusing life-sustaining treatment?
cards.b: It must be in writing, signed by the person (or on their behalf in their presence) and witnessed, with a statement that it applies even if life is at risk. The maker must have been 18 or over with capacity.

cards.f: What are the Fraser guidelines for?
cards.b: Deciding whether to provide contraceptive advice or treatment to under-16s without parental knowledge: the young person understands the advice, cannot be persuaded to tell their parents (or let the doctor do so), is likely to have sex anyway, their physical or mental health is likely to suffer without it, and it is in their best interests.

cards.f: When may confidential information be disclosed without consent?
cards.b: When required by law (e.g. notifiable diseases), or when justified in the public interest because the risk of serious harm to others outweighs the interest in confidentiality (W v Egdell 1990).

cards.f: Can a spouse consent to treatment on behalf of an adult who lacks capacity?
cards.b: No, unless they are a health and welfare attorney under a valid LPA or a court-appointed deputy. Otherwise clinicians decide in best interests after consulting them.

cards.f: What are the four domains of Good Medical Practice (2024)?
cards.b: Knowledge, skills and development; patients, partnership and communication; colleagues, culture and safety; trust and professionalism.

cards.f: What does SPIKES stand for?
cards.b: Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Emotions (empathy), Strategy and summary (Baile et al., 2000).

cards.f: Give the stages of the Calgary–Cambridge guide.
cards.b: Initiating the session, gathering information, physical examination, explanation and planning, closing the session, with providing structure and building the relationship throughout.

cards.f: What is ICE?
cards.b: Ideas, concerns and expectations: exploring the patient's perspective on their problem.

cards.f: Statutory vs professional duty of candour?
cards.b: The statutory duty (reg 20, 2014 Regulations) falls on CQC-registered organisations for notifiable safety incidents. The professional duty (GMC/NMC) falls on every individual clinician to be open and apologise when things go wrong.

cards.f: Is an apology an admission of liability?
cards.b: No. Section 2 of the Compensation Act 2006 provides that an apology or offer of treatment is not in itself an admission of negligence or breach of statutory duty.

cards.f: What protects NHS whistleblowers?
cards.b: The Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 protects workers making protected disclosures from detriment. NHS trusts also have Freedom to Speak Up Guardians.

cards.f: State the elements of gross negligence manslaughter (R v Adomako 1995).
cards.b: A duty of care, breach of that duty, the breach causing death, and the breach being so bad as to be judged criminal (gross).

cards.f: What is teach-back?
cards.b: Asking patients to explain in their own words what they have been told, to check understanding and correct misunderstandings.

cards.f: Why should family members not usually act as interpreters?
cards.b: Risks include inaccurate translation, filtering of information, breach of confidentiality, and pressure on the patient. Children should never be used. Professional interpreters should be booked.

questions.q: Researchers want to investigate possible causes of a very rare cancer with a long latent period. Which design is most efficient?
questions.why: Case-control studies sample on outcome, so rare diseases with long latency can be studied without following huge populations for decades.

questions.q: A study finds that countries with higher average chocolate consumption win more Nobel prizes per head. Concluding that individuals who eat more chocolate are more likely to win is an example of:
questions.why: The data are at country level. Inferring an individual-level relationship from group-level correlation is the ecological fallacy.

questions.q: Distinguish bias from confounding, giving a clinical example of each. (4 marks)
markScheme: Bias is systematic error in selection of participants or measurement of exposure/outcome
Valid example of bias (e.g. recall bias in mothers of children with birth defects)
Confounding is distortion by a third factor associated with both exposure and outcome and not on the causal pathway
Valid example of confounding (e.g. smoking confounding the alcohol–lung cancer association)
questions.modelAnswer: Bias is systematic error arising from how participants are selected or how information is collected. For example, in a case-control study, mothers of babies with congenital anomalies may recall medication use in pregnancy more thoroughly than control mothers (recall bias). Confounding is a mixing of effects: a third variable is associated with the exposure, independently causes the outcome, and is not on the causal pathway. For example, heavy drinkers smoke more, so an apparent link between alcohol and lung cancer may be due to smoking. Bias is mostly prevented by design. Confounding can also be adjusted for in analysis.

questions.q: Dr Amara Okafor, a public health registrar, is asked whether night-shift work increases the risk of breast cancer among nurses. Funding is limited, and she has access to (a) a national cancer registry, (b) NHS employment records going back 25 years, and (c) a large existing cohort of 60,000 female health workers recruited in 2001 with baseline questionnaires on occupation and lifestyle. Discuss the study designs she could use, the main sources of bias and confounding in each, and recommend an approach. (16 marks)
markScheme: Identifies case-control option: cases from registry, controls from nurses without cancer
Notes case-control efficiency for an outcome with long latency; gives odds ratio
Identifies recall bias / differential exposure measurement in case-control if self-reported; reduced if employment records used
Discusses selection of controls (same source population)
Identifies cohort option using existing 2001 cohort (prospective data) or retrospective cohort via employment records
Cohort advantages: temporality, incidence, RR, exposure measured before outcome
Cohort limitations: loss to follow-up, exposure misclassification as shift patterns change, healthy worker effect
Confounders named: age, parity/age at first birth, HRT/oral contraceptive use, alcohol, BMI, family history, screening attendance
Methods to handle confounding: matching, stratification, multivariable regression
Notes RCT is unethical/infeasible
Mentions dose–response (years of night work) and Bradford Hill reasoning
Reasoned recommendation, e.g. nested case-control or cohort analysis within the existing cohort linked to the registry
questions.modelAnswer:
An RCT is impossible: nurses cannot be randomised to decades of night work. Dr Okafor must use an observational design.

A case-control study would take breast cancer cases among nurses from the registry and compare them with nurses from the same source population who are cancer-free. It is efficient for an outcome with a long latency and gives an odds ratio. If exposure comes from interviews, recall bias is a risk, because women with cancer may recall shift patterns differently. Using contemporaneous employment records avoids this. Controls must come from the same base population, or selection bias follows.

A cohort design is stronger on temporality. The existing 2001 cohort recorded occupation and lifestyle before diagnosis, and linkage to the cancer registry identifies outcomes, giving incidence and relative risk. A retrospective cohort built from employment records is another option. The weaknesses are exposure misclassification (shift patterns change, so one baseline measure is crude), loss to follow-up, and the healthy worker effect.

In both designs the key confounders include age, parity and age at first birth, use of hormonal contraception or HRT, alcohol, BMI, family history, and screening uptake, since more screening finds more cancer. These can be addressed by matching (age), stratification and multivariable regression. Residual confounding, for example by unmeasured light exposure or sleep, will remain.

She should look for a dose–response relationship with cumulative years of night work, which supports causation under Bradford Hill's biological gradient.

Recommendation: a nested case-control study within the 2001 cohort, linked to the registry and to employment records. It combines prospectively recorded exposure (no recall bias, clear temporality) with the cost efficiency of studying only cases and a sample of controls. Detailed shift histories can then be extracted from employment records for this smaller group.

questions.q: In a trial, 20% of patients in the placebo group and 15% in the treatment group have a stroke over five years. What is the number needed to treat to prevent one stroke over five years?
Define incidence and prevalence, and explain why the introduction of an effective life-prolonging (but not curative) treatment would increase prevalence. (3 marks)
markScheme: Incidence: new cases in a population at risk over a specified period
Prevalence: proportion of a population with the disease at a point/period
Prevalence ≈ incidence × duration, so longer survival with disease raises prevalence even if incidence is unchanged
questions.modelAnswer: Incidence is the number of new cases arising in a population at risk during a specified period, expressed as a proportion or a rate per person-time. Prevalence is the proportion of a population who have the disease at a given point or during a period. In a steady state, prevalence is approximately incidence multiplied by average disease duration. A treatment that prolongs survival without curing the disease lengthens duration. People live with the condition for longer, so prevalence rises even though incidence is unchanged, as happened with antiretroviral therapy for HIV.

questions.q: In a cohort study, 30 of 1,000 smokers and 20 of 2,000 non-smokers develop disease X. Calculate (a) the relative risk, (b) the risk difference, (c) the number needed to harm, (d) the attributable fraction among smokers, and (e) the population attributable fraction. (5 marks)
markScheme: Risk difference = 2 percentage points (0.02)
AF exposed = (3 − 1)/3 = 67%
questions.modelAnswer: Risk in smokers = 30/1,000 = 3%; risk in non-smokers = 20/2,000 = 1%. (a) RR = 3/1 = 3. (b) Risk difference = 3% − 1% = 2 percentage points. (c) NNH = 1/0.02 = 50: for every 50 people who smoke, one extra case occurs over the study period. (d) Attributable fraction among smokers = (RR − 1)/RR = 2/3 ≈ 67%. (e) The proportion exposed is 1,000/3,000 = 1/3, so PAF = (1/3 × 2)/(1 + 2/3) = 0.4. Check: overall risk = 50/3,000 = 1.67%, and (1.67 − 1)/1.67 = 0.4. If the association is causal, 40% of cases in this population are attributable to smoking.

questions.q: A case-control study investigates whether regular use of an over-the-counter sleep aid is associated with hip fracture in adults over 70. There are 100 cases and 200 controls. Sixty cases and 50 controls report regular use. (a) Construct the 2×2 table and calculate the odds ratio. (b) Calculate an approximate 95% confidence interval using the standard error of the log odds ratio (Woolf's method) and interpret it. (c) Explain why the odds ratio approximates the relative risk here. (d) Discuss three alternative explanations for the association other than causation. (15 marks)
markScheme: Correct table: cases exposed 60, unexposed 40; controls exposed 50, unexposed 150
Interpretation: CI excludes 1, so association statistically significant at 5% level; strong association
Rare disease assumption: hip fracture is uncommon in the population, so odds ≈ risk
Chance considered and largely excluded by CI
Recall bias: cases may recall medication use more thoroughly
Selection bias in controls (e.g. hospital controls with conditions linked to drug use)
Confounding, e.g. frailty, dementia, other sedatives, alcohol, falls history (confounding by indication)
Reverse causation unlikely but timing of exposure must precede fracture
Suggests remedies: prescription records, matching, multivariable adjustment
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Exposed: 60 cases, 50 controls. Unexposed: 40 cases, 150 controls. OR = (60 × 150)/(40 × 50) = 9,000/2,000 = 4.5. The odds of regular sleep-aid use are 4.5 times higher in people with hip fracture than in controls.

(b) ln(4.5) = 1.504. SE = √(1/60 + 1/40 + 1/50 + 1/150) = √(0.0167 + 0.0250 + 0.0200 + 0.0067) = √0.0683 = 0.261. 1.96 × 0.261 = 0.512, so the 95% CI = exp(0.992) to exp(2.016), which is about 2.7 to 7.5. The interval excludes 1, so chance is an unlikely explanation at the 5% level. Even the lower bound suggests a substantial association, although the interval is wide because the sample is small.

(c) In a case-control study risks cannot be calculated, because the investigator fixed the 1:2 ratio of cases to controls. When the outcome is rare in the source population, as hip fracture is over a short period, odds and risks are almost equal, so the OR approximates the RR (the rare disease assumption).

(d) Alternative explanations:
- Recall bias: people who have had a fracture may search their memories for causes and report medicine use more completely. Using pharmacy or GP prescribing records would reduce this.
- Selection bias: if controls were hospital patients, or community volunteers who are fitter than average, their exposure prevalence may not reflect the source population.
- Confounding: people taking sleep aids may be frailer, have dementia, nocturia, other sedatives or alcohol use, all of which increase falls. This is confounding by indication. Matching and multivariable adjustment help, but residual confounding remains.
- Temporality must be confirmed: exposure has to come before the fracture.

A dose–response relationship, consistent findings in other studies and a plausible mechanism (sedation and postural instability) would strengthen a causal interpretation.

questions.q: The classic criteria for a screening programme were published in 1968 for the World Health Organization by:
questions.why: Wilson and Jungner's 'Principles and practice of screening for disease' (WHO, 1968) set out the ten classic criteria.

questions.q: Explain lead-time bias, length-time bias and overdiagnosis in screening. (3 marks)
markScheme: Lead-time bias: earlier diagnosis lengthens apparent survival from diagnosis without delaying death
Length-time bias: slow-growing disease spends longer in detectable phase, so screening over-detects favourable-prognosis cases
Overdiagnosis: detecting disease that would never have caused symptoms or death, leading to unnecessary treatment
questions.modelAnswer: Lead-time bias: screening moves the date of diagnosis earlier, so survival measured from diagnosis looks longer even if the person dies at the same time as they would have without screening. Length-time bias: indolent tumours stay in the pre-clinical detectable phase for longer than aggressive ones, so screen-detected cases are weighted towards better prognosis. Overdiagnosis: screening finds disease, such as some ductal carcinoma in situ or low-grade prostate cancer, that would never have caused symptoms or death. Those people receive treatment and its harms without benefit. All three make screening look more effective than it is.

questions.q: A new blood test for a cancer has sensitivity 90% and specificity 95%. A health board proposes using it to screen 10,000 asymptomatic adults in whom the prevalence of the cancer is 1%. (a) Construct the 2×2 table and calculate the PPV and NPV. (b) Recalculate the PPV if the same test were used in a symptomatic clinic population of 10,000 with prevalence 10%. (c) Using your results, advise the board on whether to proceed with population screening, considering both test performance and wider screening criteria. (14 marks)
markScheme: Diseased 100: TP 90, FN 10
Non-diseased 9,900: TN 9,405, FP 495
At 10%: diseased 1,000, TP 900, FN 100; non-diseased 9,000, FP 450, TN 8,550
Explains that PPV depends on prevalence; sensitivity/specificity unchanged
Harms of false positives: anxiety, invasive follow-up, cost
False negatives (10 missed) and false reassurance
Need RCT evidence that screening reduces mortality; lead-time/length-time/overdiagnosis
Applies Wilson–Jungner/UK NSC criteria (treatment, natural history, acceptability, cost, capacity)
Reasoned recommendation, e.g. not yet; pilot/RCT or targeted high-risk screening
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Of 10,000 people, 100 have the cancer. With 90% sensitivity, TP = 90 and FN = 10. Of the 9,900 without it, 95% specificity gives TN = 9,405 and FP = 495. PPV = 90/(90 + 495) = 90/585 = 15.4%. NPV = 9,405/(9,405 + 10) = 99.9%.

(b) At 10% prevalence: 1,000 have the cancer (TP 900, FN 100) and 9,000 do not (TN 8,550, FP 450). PPV = 900/1,350 = 66.7%. The test is unchanged, but PPV rises sharply because true positives now outnumber false positives.

(c) In the screening population, about 85% of positive results are false. Some 495 well people would face anxiety and invasive investigation (perhaps imaging or biopsy, with their own complications) for every 90 cancers found, and 10 cancers would be missed, with possible false reassurance. Before proceeding, the UK NSC would expect:
- evidence from randomised trials that screen-detection reduces cancer-specific mortality, rather than improving survival from diagnosis, which is inflated by lead-time and length-time bias
- an understanding of natural history and of how much overdiagnosis occurs
- an effective treatment that works better when started early
- an agreed pathway and capacity for diagnostic follow-up
- acceptability to the public, and cost-effectiveness against other uses of resources
- arrangements for informed choice and quality assurance.

Recommendation: do not introduce population screening on these figures alone. The board could use the test as a diagnostic aid in symptomatic or high-risk groups, where the PPV is acceptable, and support a pilot or RCT measuring mortality, harms and cost-effectiveness before considering a population programme.

questions.q: 'Screening healthy people always does more good than harm, because finding disease early can only help.' Critically evaluate this proposition with reference to the principles of screening and to UK screening programmes. (20 marks)
markScheme: Defines screening and distinguishes from diagnosis/case-finding
Sets out Wilson–Jungner (1968) / UK NSC criteria
Explains benefits where good evidence exists (e.g. bowel: gFOBT RCTs; AAA: MASS trial; cervical: strong observational evidence of reduced incidence and mortality)
Explains lead-time and length-time bias making early detection appear beneficial
Explains overdiagnosis and overtreatment, with breast screening example (Independent UK Panel 2012: about 3 overdiagnosed per death prevented)
PSA testing as example: no population programme because harms outweigh uncertain benefit (UK NSC 2026 recommended only targeted screening for BRCA2 carriers with a family history)
False positives, false reassurance, psychological harm, opportunity cost
PPV dependence on prevalence in low-risk populations
Informed choice rather than uptake as an ethical aim; autonomy
Equity: uptake gradients may widen inequalities
Need for quality assurance and whole-pathway capacity
Balanced conclusion rejecting 'always' but recognising net benefit of well-evidenced programmes
questions.modelAnswer:
The proposition is intuitively attractive but wrong as a general claim. Screening intervenes on healthy people, so the ethical bar is higher than in clinical medicine: the programme initiates contact and implicitly promises benefit.

Wilson and Jungner (1968), and the UK NSC's modern criteria, require more than early detection: an important condition with known natural history and a detectable early phase; an acceptable test; effective treatment that works better early; capacity, agreed policy and cost-effectiveness; and randomised evidence that benefits outweigh harms.

Where evidence exists, screening helps. Cervical screening prevents cancer by treating precancerous change. Bowel screening reduces colorectal cancer mortality, shown in randomised trials of guaiac faecal occult blood testing; the programme now uses the more sensitive FIT. AAA ultrasound for men aged 65 was supported by the MASS trial.

Yet early detection is not automatically beneficial. Lead-time bias lengthens survival from diagnosis without delaying death. Length-time bias over-samples indolent disease. Overdiagnosis means treating disease that would never have caused harm. The Independent UK Panel (2012) concluded that breast screening reduces mortality, but estimated about three overdiagnosed women per death prevented, a trade-off that must be communicated honestly. PSA testing shows why the UK does not screen all men for prostate cancer: false positives, biopsy complications and overtreatment weigh against uncertain mortality benefit. In 2026 the UK NSC recommended only targeted screening for a small high-risk group (men with a BRCA2 variant and a family history).

In low-prevalence populations even good tests have low PPV, so many well people receive false alarms and invasive follow-up. False negatives falsely reassure. Programmes carry opportunity costs. Uptake gradients by deprivation and ethnicity can widen inequalities unless outreach is built in.

Modern UK practice therefore aims at informed choice rather than maximum uptake, respecting autonomy through balanced natural-frequency information.

Conclusion: screening does more good than harm only when a programme meets rigorous criteria, is quality-assured across the whole pathway and is offered with honest information. 'Always' is false. Early detection is valuable only when it changes outcomes.

questions.q: A trial reports p = 0.03 for its primary outcome. Which statement is correct?
options: There is a 97% chance the treatment works
If there were truly no difference, results at least this extreme would occur about 3% of the time
There is a 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true
The treatment effect is clinically important
questions.why: The p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true. It says nothing directly about clinical importance or the probability that the hypothesis is true.

questions.q: An investigator compares the proportion of patients readmitted within 30 days (yes/no) between two independent groups of 400 patients each. Which test is most appropriate?
questions.why: Comparing proportions of a binary outcome between independent groups with large expected counts calls for a chi-squared test.

questions.q: In a sample of 36 adults the mean systolic blood pressure is 140 mmHg with a standard deviation of 12 mmHg. (a) Calculate the standard error. (b) Calculate the 95% confidence interval for the mean. (c) Interpret the interval. (d) State how the interval would change if the sample were 144 people with the same SD. (4 marks)
markScheme: SE = 12/√36 = 2 mmHg
Interpretation: range of plausible values for the population mean; 95% of such intervals would contain the true mean
n = 144: SE = 1, CI halves in width to 138.0–142.0 mmHg
questions.modelAnswer: (a) SE = SD/√n = 12/6 = 2 mmHg. (b) 95% CI = 140 ± 1.96 × 2 = 140 ± 3.92, which is 136.1 to 143.9 mmHg. (c) The interval gives a range of plausible values for the true population mean. If the sampling were repeated many times, 95% of intervals built this way would contain the true mean. (d) With n = 144, SE = 12/12 = 1, so the CI is 140 ± 1.96, about 138.0 to 142.0 mmHg. Quadrupling the sample halves the width.

questions.q: A trial randomised 4,000 adults with a history of myocardial infarction to a new lipid-lowering drug class (n = 2,000) or placebo (n = 2,000). Over three years the primary composite outcome (cardiovascular death, MI or stroke) occurred in 160 patients on the drug and 200 on placebo: hazard ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.64–0.97, p = 0.03. 160 patients stopped the drug because of side effects. The authors' per-protocol analysis gave a hazard ratio of 0.70. A subgroup analysis suggested benefit only in women (p = 0.02 for women, p = 0.30 for men). (a) Calculate the absolute risk reduction, relative risk reduction and NNT. (b) Critically appraise the results and the authors' conclusion that 'the drug should be offered to all post-MI patients, especially women'. (16 marks)
markScheme: Risks: 8% vs 10%
ARR = 2 percentage points
NNT = 50 over 3 years
HR CI excludes 1 but upper limit near 1: effect may be small; statistically significant at 5%
Clinical significance: weigh NNT 50 against harms, cost; composite outcome components should be examined
ITT is the primary analysis; per-protocol inflates benefit and breaks randomisation
Discontinuation due to adverse effects (8%) indicates tolerability issues; NNH relevant
Subgroup claim: different p-values do not show a difference between subgroups; need test of interaction, pre-specification, biological plausibility; likely chance
Multiple comparisons risk
Generalisability: trial population, follow-up duration, funding/conflicts
Conclusion: modest benefit; offering to all may be reasonable after shared decision-making, but 'especially women' unsupported
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Event risk on the drug = 160/2,000 = 8%; on placebo = 200/2,000 = 10%. ARR = 2 percentage points; RR = 0.8, so RRR = 20%. NNT = 1/0.02 = 50: fifty patients must be treated for three years to prevent one composite event.

(b) Appraisal:
- The intention-to-treat hazard ratio of 0.79 (95% CI 0.64–0.97) is statistically significant, but the upper limit is close to 1. The data are compatible with anything from a substantial to a trivial benefit. A p-value of 0.03 is fragile, and a few events either way could remove significance.
- Clinical importance depends on context. An NNT of 50 over three years is comparable to some established secondary prevention treatments, but it must be weighed against harms and cost. The composite outcome should be broken down: if the benefit is driven by non-fatal MI rather than death, the case is weaker.
- 160 patients (8%) stopped because of side effects. That is a tolerability signal, and an NNH should be reported for serious adverse events.
- The per-protocol HR of 0.70 cannot be preferred. Excluding people who stopped removes those who could not tolerate the drug, breaks randomisation and inflates benefit. ITT reflects real-world effectiveness and is the primary analysis in a superiority trial.
- The subgroup claim is unsound. 'Significant in women, not in men' is not evidence of a difference between them; a formal test of interaction is needed. Was the subgroup pre-specified? Is there biological plausibility? With multiple subgroups, one 'significant' result is expected by chance. Subgroup findings should be treated as hypothesis-generating.
- Generalisability depends on inclusion criteria, adherence, length of follow-up and funding source.

Conclusion: the trial suggests a modest relative and absolute benefit of uncertain size. Offering the drug through shared decision-making, explaining the NNT and side effects, is defensible. A recommendation of 'especially women' is unsupported, and the authors overstate their results.

questions.q: The 'inverse care law', stating that the availability of good medical care tends to vary inversely with the need for it, was described by:
questions.why: Julian Tudor Hart, a Welsh GP, set out the inverse care law in the Lancet in 1971.

questions.q: Explain the concept of proportionate universalism and give one example of how it could be applied in the NHS. (4 marks)
markScheme: Originates from the Marmot Review 'Fair Society, Healthy Lives' (2010)
Actions are universal (offered to all)
Scale and intensity proportionate to level of disadvantage
Valid example, e.g. universal health visiting with additional visits for deprived families; or targeted outreach within a universal screening programme
questions.modelAnswer: Proportionate universalism comes from the Marmot Review, 'Fair Society, Healthy Lives' (2010). Focusing only on the most disadvantaged would miss the social gradient, which affects everyone below the top. So actions should be universal, but delivered with a scale and intensity proportionate to the level of disadvantage. For example, the healthy child programme offers health visiting to all families, with more frequent visits, parenting support and linked services for families in deprived areas or with identified needs. Another example is adding text reminders, outreach and community champions to bowel screening in areas with low uptake.

questions.q: Using the explanations set out in the Black Report (1980), discuss why the social gradient in health persists in the UK. Illustrate your answer with evidence. (14 marks)
markScheme: Defines social gradient (Whitehall studies)
Artefact explanation explained and largely rejected (gradient persists with different measures)
Natural/social selection: health-related mobility; evidence it contributes only modestly
Cultural/behavioural: smoking, diet, alcohol patterned by class
Notes behaviours explain only part of gradient (Whitehall: risk factors explained a minority)
Materialist/structural: income, housing, employment, environment
Psychosocial pathways: control at work, stress (Whitehall II)
Life-course perspective / early years
Marmot 2010 and 2020 evidence of persistence and widening
Interaction: behaviours shaped by material circumstances ('causes of the causes')
Concluding judgement
questions.modelAnswer:
The social gradient is the stepwise worsening of health down the social hierarchy. The Whitehall studies showed it among civil servants, none of whom were poor in absolute terms. The Black Report (1980) offered four explanations, and they still frame the debate.

Artefact: the gradient might be an artefact of how class is measured, for instance shrinking manual classes exaggerating differences. But gradients appear with income, education, area deprivation (IMD) and occupation, and in life expectancy and healthy life expectancy, so artefact cannot explain them.

Natural or social selection: ill health may cause downward mobility, as when chronic illness leads to job loss. Longitudinal studies suggest health selection contributes, but modestly. Childhood circumstances predict adult health independent of adult class.

Cultural or behavioural: smoking, poor diet, inactivity and harmful drinking are more common in deprived groups, and smoking is a major contributor to differences in life expectancy. Yet in Whitehall I, conventional risk factors explained only part of the gradient in coronary mortality. Behaviours are themselves socially patterned by stress, marketing, access to affordable healthy food and the immediacy of other pressures.

Materialist or structural: income, housing quality, work conditions, pollution, neighbourhood safety and access to services directly affect health. The Black Report favoured this explanation. Whitehall II added a psychosocial pathway: low control at work and effort–reward imbalance predicted coronary disease. A life-course view explains how disadvantage accumulates from early childhood.

Persistence: the Marmot Review (2010) set out six policy objectives, and its 2020 follow-up found life expectancy improvements had stalled and inequalities widened. It linked this to austerity and child poverty. The inverse care law adds a health service dimension.

Conclusion: the gradient persists because the material and psychosocial conditions that generate it persist. Behavioural differences are better seen as pathways ('causes of the causes') than as root causes. This is why upstream, cross-government policy matters more than health service action alone.

questions.q: 'Health inequalities are primarily the result of individual lifestyle choices, so the main policy response should be health education.' Critically evaluate this claim. (20 marks)
markScheme: Defines health inequalities/inequity
Acknowledges contribution of behaviours (smoking, alcohol, diet) to mortality differences
Challenges 'choice': behaviours socially patterned and constrained by environment/income/stress
Whitehall evidence that risk factors explain only part of the gradient
Dahlgren and Whitehead model: wider determinants
Black Report materialist explanation; Marmot 2010 six objectives and 2020 widening
Intervention-generated inequalities: education campaigns benefit advantaged most
Structural/population interventions (smoking ban, tobacco tax, Soft Drinks Industry Levy, minimum unit pricing in Scotland) may reduce gaps
Proportionate universalism
Ethical analysis: responsibility, autonomy vs justice, victim-blaming
Role of NHS: inverse care law, Core20PLUS5, statutory duties
Balanced conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Health inequalities are systematic, avoidable differences in health between social groups. The claim contains some truth. Smoking is a leading contributor to the life-expectancy gap between rich and poor, alcohol, diet and inactivity add to it, and health education supports informed choice.

The claim nonetheless fails on three counts.

First, 'choice' is socially structured. Dahlgren and Whitehead's model places behaviour inside layers of community, living and working conditions, and wider socioeconomic conditions. Smoking tracks deprivation, stress, retail environments and marketing. Healthy food costs more per calorie, and safe green space is unevenly distributed. Behaviours are pathways for disadvantage, the 'causes of the causes'.

Second, behaviour is not the primary driver. In Whitehall I, conventional risk factors explained only part of the coronary gradient by grade. Whitehall II implicated low job control. The Black Report (1980) favoured materialist explanations. Marmot (2010) called for action on early years, work, income, places and prevention, and the 2020 review linked stalled life expectancy to wider social and economic conditions.

Third, education-led policy can widen gaps. Campaigns depend on literacy, time, money and a sense of control, so advantaged groups benefit most (intervention-generated inequality). Structural measures tend to work across groups: smoke-free legislation, tobacco taxation, the Soft Drinks Industry Levy and minimum unit pricing for alcohol in Scotland.

Ethically, an exclusive lifestyle focus risks victim-blaming. It shifts responsibility for structural injustice onto individuals and neglects justice. Respecting autonomy requires real options, not just information.

Health services matter too. The inverse care law describes unequal access and quality. NHS bodies have statutory duties to have regard to reducing inequalities, and Core20PLUS5 targets the most deprived 20%.

Conclusion: lifestyle is a proximate mechanism, not the primary cause. The best response is proportionate universalism: upstream structural policy, accessible services and targeted support, with health education as one modest component.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a condition of the doctrine of double effect?
options: The bad effect must not be the means by which the good effect is achieved
There must be a proportionate reason for allowing the bad effect
The act itself must be good or morally neutral
The patient must have given written consent to the bad effect
questions.why: The classical conditions concern the nature of the act, intention, means and proportionality. Written consent is not one of them.

questions.q: Explain the difference between act and rule utilitarianism and show how each might approach a doctor's decision about breaching confidentiality to prevent minor harm to a third party. (4 marks)
markScheme: Act utilitarianism judges each individual act by its consequences
Act utilitarian might breach if the immediate net benefit is greater
Rule utilitarianism follows rules whose general observance maximises good
Rule utilitarian would likely keep confidence because a general rule of confidentiality sustains trust and disclosure, giving better outcomes overall
questions.modelAnswer: Act utilitarianism assesses each action by its own consequences: the right act maximises overall welfare in that situation. Faced with a chance to prevent minor harm to a third party, an act utilitarian might breach confidentiality if the immediate benefit seemed to outweigh the harm to the patient. Rule utilitarianism asks which general rules, if followed, produce the best outcomes. A rule of medical confidentiality encourages patients to seek care and disclose sensitive information, which benefits public health overall. So a rule utilitarian would keep the confidence where the threatened harm is minor, and allow exceptions only for serious harm. This mirrors GMC guidance.

questions.q: An integrated care board must decide whether to fund a new targeted therapy for a rare childhood cancer. It costs far more per QALY than the ICB normally accepts, and the evidence comes from a small single-arm study. The parents of Leo, a seven-year-old with relapsed disease, have launched a media campaign. A local GP argues that the same money could fund a hypertension case-finding programme in deprived neighbourhoods. Analyse the ethical issues and advise the ICB on how to reach a defensible decision. (18 marks)
markScheme: Identifies justice/distributive question and opportunity cost
Explains QALY and cost-effectiveness approach (utilitarian)
Critiques QALY: ageism, disability, rarity, poor evidence
Rule of rescue and identifiable vs statistical lives
Uncertainty of evidence (single-arm study) relevant to beneficence/non-maleficence
Equity considerations: deprived groups (Core20PLUS5) and health inequalities
Children/end-of-life weighting arguments
Procedural justice: Daniels and Sabin accountability for reasonableness (publicity, relevance, revisability, enforcement)
Legal context: courts reluctant to interfere if rational and procedurally fair (R v Cambridge HA ex p B 1995)
Consistency: avoid media-driven exceptions; individual funding request route with exceptionality
Compassion and communication with Leo's family
Defended conclusion/advice
questions.modelAnswer:
This is a problem of distributive justice under scarcity: every pound spent on the therapy is unavailable for other care.

A consequentialist approach uses cost per QALY to maximise health gain from a fixed budget. Case-finding could prevent many strokes and heart attacks cheaply, and it targets deprived groups, which serves the equity duty and Core20PLUS5. On these grounds it looks the better buy.

The QALY has known limits. It may undervalue gains for children or people with disability, struggles with rare diseases whose trials are necessarily small, and treats every QALY as equal. Some argue society values treating severe illness more highly, and NICE now uses a severity modifier. The rule of rescue pulls strongly towards Leo, an identifiable child, while the beneficiaries of case-finding are 'statistical' lives. That pull is understandable but a poor basis for policy, because it favours the visible.

The weak evidence matters. A single-arm study cannot reliably show benefit, so funding risks harm and false hope (non-maleficence). The uncertainty may justify access within a trial or data-collection arrangement rather than routine funding.

Because reasonable people disagree, procedural justice is central. Daniels and Sabin's accountability for reasonableness requires reasons that are public and relevant, open to appeal and revision, and enforced. The ICB should apply its published policy consistently, and judge any individual funding request on clinical exceptionality, not media pressure, which would be unfair to quieter patients. Courts will not override a rational, fair process (R v Cambridge HA, ex p B, 1995).

Advice: decide through the established process, weighing evidence, cost-effectiveness, severity, equity and opportunity cost, and record the reasons. Explore national routes such as specialised commissioning, trials or managed access. Communicate compassionately with Leo's family, offering appeal and oncology and palliative support. If the therapy is declined, case-finding is likely the more defensible use of these funds.

questions.q: 'Respect for patient autonomy should always take priority over beneficence.' Discuss with reference to ethical theory, English law and clinical examples. (20 marks)
markScheme: Defines autonomy (self-determination; Kantian and Millian roots) and beneficence
Notes four principles are prima facie with no fixed hierarchy
Legal support for autonomy: capacitous refusal (Re T 1992, Re B 2002, St George's v S 1998)
Montgomery 2015 shift from paternalism to patient-centred disclosure
Limits: autonomy requires capacity (MCA 2005); best interests where lacking
Autonomy does not entitle patients to demand treatment (R (Burke) v GMC 2005)
Mental Health Act permits treatment without consent for mental disorder: beneficence/protection overrides
Children: courts overriding refusals (Re W 1992); welfare paramount
Third-party harm limits autonomy (confidentiality exceptions; public health)
Relational autonomy critique; unwise decisions vs undermined autonomy (coercion, depression)
Assisted suicide prohibition (Nicklinson) shows law limits autonomy
Reasoned conclusion: strong presumption but not absolute
questions.modelAnswer:
Autonomy is the capacity for self-governance, drawing on Kant (persons as ends in themselves) and Mill (the harm principle). Beneficence is the duty to promote the patient's good. Beauchamp and Childress treat both as prima facie, so neither automatically wins.

English law gives autonomy great weight. A capacitous adult may refuse treatment for rational, irrational or no reasons, even if death follows (Re T 1992; Re B 2002), and pregnancy changes nothing (St George's v S 1998). Montgomery (2015) rejected paternalism in disclosure. Under the MCA 2005 an unwise decision is not proof of incapacity. In refusal cases, autonomy does prevail, and overriding it is battery.

But 'always' goes too far:
- Autonomy presupposes capacity. Without capacity the MCA requires best-interests decisions, which are beneficence informed by the person's values (Aintree v James 2013).
- Autonomy is mainly a right to refuse, not to demand. Doctors need not provide clinically inappropriate treatment (R (Burke) v GMC 2005).
- The Mental Health Act 1983 permits treatment for mental disorder without consent, even in some capacitous patients, a controversial legislative priority for protection.
- Courts have overridden competent minors' refusals of life-saving treatment (Re W 1992).
- Harm to others limits autonomy: confidentiality yields to serious risk (W v Egdell), and public health law can restrict liberty.
- Assisting suicide remains an offence (s2 Suicide Act 1961; Nicklinson 2014), pending any change by Parliament.

Relational accounts add that choices are shaped by illness, relationships and pressure. Respecting autonomy may mean supporting decision-making, exploring depression or coercion and allowing time, not mere deference. Properly understood, beneficence includes respect for persons.
