Conclusion: a capacitous adult's refusal carries decisive weight, but autonomy is not an absolute trump. It yields where capacity is lacking, where positive entitlements are claimed, where others are endangered and under specific statutes. 'A strong presumption' describes the position better than 'always'.

questions.q: Under s3 Mental Capacity Act 2005, which of the following is NOT one of the abilities a person must have to make a decision?
options: Justify the decision to the clinician as rational
Understand the information relevant to the decision
Use or weigh that information as part of the decision-making process
questions.why: Section 3 requires understanding, retention, using or weighing, and communication. There is no requirement to give a rational justification, and unwise decisions do not prove incapacity.

questions.q: Following Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board (2015), which statement best describes the doctor's duty when obtaining consent?
options: Disclose all risks, however small, in every case
Disclose only those risks the patient specifically asks about
Disclose the risks that a responsible body of medical opinion would disclose
Take reasonable care to ensure the patient is aware of material risks and of reasonable alternatives
questions.why: Montgomery replaced the Bolam standard for disclosure with a patient-centred materiality test, covering material risks and reasonable alternatives.

questions.q: Fifteen-year-old Jade asks her GP for the contraceptive pill and does not want her parents told. Explain the legal framework the GP should apply. (5 marks)
markScheme: Under-16 so FLRA 1969 s8 does not apply; Gillick competence applies (Gillick 1986)
Assess understanding of nature, purpose, risks and alternatives
Fraser guidelines: understands advice; cannot be persuaded to tell parents; likely to have sex anyway; physical/mental health would suffer; best interests
Confidentiality owed to competent young person; disclosure only if serious harm/safeguarding concern
Safeguarding: consider exploitation/abuse, age and power imbalance of partner; document; STI advice
questions.modelAnswer: Jade is under 16, so s8 Family Law Reform Act 1969 does not apply. She can consent if Gillick competent (1986), meaning she understands the nature, purpose, risks and alternatives. For contraception the Fraser guidelines apply. She understands the advice; she cannot be persuaded to tell her parents; she is likely to have sex anyway; her health would otherwise suffer; and treatment is in her best interests. A competent young person is owed confidentiality. The GP must still screen for safeguarding concerns such as the partner's age, coercion or exploitation, give sexual health advice and document the assessment.

questions.q: Mr Daniel Hughes, 46, a delivery van driver, has had two generalised seizures in the past month. Investigations confirm epilepsy. His neurologist, Dr Rossi, advises him that he must stop driving and inform the DVLA. Two weeks later Dr Rossi sees Mr Hughes park his van outside the clinic. Mr Hughes says he cannot afford to lose his job and asks Dr Rossi to 'keep this between us'. Advise Dr Rossi on her legal and professional obligations. (16 marks)
markScheme: Duty of confidentiality: common law, UK GDPR/DPA 2018, GMC Confidentiality (2017)
Confidentiality not absolute: consent, legal requirement, public interest
Responsibility for informing DVLA lies with the driver
First step: ensure he understands the condition, legal duty and risk; check capacity
Persuasion: discuss consequences, offer second opinion, support, involve occupational health with consent
Public interest test: risk of death/serious harm to others outweighs interest in confidentiality (W v Egdell 1990)
GMC guidance: if patient continues to drive against advice, contact DVLA medical adviser promptly
Inform patient of intention to disclose before doing so (unless unsafe/impractical) and confirm in writing afterwards
Disclose minimum necessary to DVLA medical adviser only (not employer without consent)
Document reasoning and discussions
Seek advice from Caldicott guardian/defence organisation if uncertain
Consider support: social/financial impact, employment advice, compassion
questions.modelAnswer:
Dr Rossi owes Mr Hughes a duty of confidentiality at common law, under UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018, and professionally (GMC, 'Confidentiality', 2017). The duty is not absolute. Disclosure can be justified with consent, by legal requirement, or in the public interest where others face a risk of death or serious harm that outweighs the interest in confidentiality (W v Egdell 1990).

The legal duty to notify the DVLA rests with the driver. GMC guidance suggests a staged approach.

1. Make sure he understands that epilepsy affects his fitness to drive, that he must tell the DVLA, and that a seizure at the wheel could kill him and others. Check his capacity. If he disputes the diagnosis, offer a second opinion, advising him not to drive meanwhile.
2. Persuade. Explore his employment fears, signpost occupational health, employment advice and welfare support, suggest he involve his family, and record the discussion.
3. Because he continues to drive a delivery van against advice, the public interest justifies disclosure. Dr Rossi should promptly contact the DVLA's medical adviser, disclosing only relevant information.
4. Tell him before disclosing, unless unsafe or impracticable, and confirm in writing afterwards.
5. Do not contact his employer without consent. The DVLA is the proper recipient, and wider disclosure would breach confidentiality.
6. Document the reasoning, and seek advice from her defence organisation or the Caldicott guardian if unsure.

Throughout she should be compassionate. The loss of income is real, and keeping the therapeutic relationship supports adherence to treatment, which may in time restore his entitlement to drive.

questions.q: Mrs Harriet Lowe, 82, has moderate vascular dementia and lives in a care home. She is admitted with a fractured neck of femur. The orthopaedic team recommends hip surgery. Mrs Lowe repeatedly says 'no operations, I want to go home', but cannot recall from one minute to the next that she has broken her hip. Her son, who says he is her 'next of kin', insists she have the surgery. Her daughter says their mother always said she 'never wanted to end up in hospital'. There is no LPA or advance decision on file. Advise the team on how the law governs the decision. (20 marks)
markScheme: Applies MCA 2005 principles: presumption of capacity, all practicable steps, unwise decision
Decision-specific and time-specific assessment by the clinician proposing treatment
Functional test s3 first (JB 2021): cannot retain/understand/weigh information about the fracture and options
Causative nexus s2: inability caused by dementia (impairment of mind/brain)
Support steps: simple explanation, aids, timing, family involvement, repeated attempts; document
Son as 'next of kin' has no legal power to consent; no LPA/deputy
Best interests s4: consider past and present wishes, feelings, beliefs and values (including daughter's account and current objection), consult family and carers
Weigh clinical factors: surgery offers pain relief, mobility, lower mortality vs anaesthetic risk; non-operative management consequences
Aintree v James (2013): consider patient's perspective; holistic welfare
Less restrictive option; managing objection/restraint s6 (proportionate, necessary)
IMCA s37 needed only if no one appropriate to consult (here family exists); consider if family conflict
Disputes: second opinion, best-interests meeting, ethics committee; Court of Protection if unresolved; DoLS consideration
questions.modelAnswer:
The Mental Capacity Act 2005 governs this decision.

Capacity. Mrs Lowe is presumed to have capacity (s1(2)). Dementia alone does not prove incapacity, nor does an unwise refusal. The surgeon proposing the operation should assess capacity for this decision now, after all practicable steps to help her (s1(3)): plain language, hearing aids and glasses, a calm setting, her most lucid time of day, familiar carers and repeated attempts.

Following JB [2021] UKSC 52, the functional question comes first (s3). Can she understand, retain, use or weigh the information (the fracture, the surgery, its risks and benefits, the consequences of refusing) and communicate a decision? Brief retention suffices if she can decide within it (s3(3)), but she cannot hold the fact of the fracture long enough to weigh options. The team must then find that this inability is caused by her vascular dementia (s2), and document reasons.

Who decides. 'Next of kin' gives her son no power to consent. With no LPA, deputy or advance decision, the treating clinician decides in her best interests (ss4–5).

Best interests. The clinician must weigh her current objection and wish to go home, her long-held views as the daughter reports them, her values, and the views of both children and care home staff, seeing the decision from her perspective (Aintree v James 2013). Surgery usually offers the best pain relief and chance of walking, and so of returning home. Non-operative care risks prolonged immobility and complications. These must be balanced against anaesthetic risk. A best-interests meeting with family, anaesthetist and geriatrician is wise.

Safeguards. Any restraint must be necessary and proportionate (s6), using the less restrictive option. Prolonged confinement may need DoLS authorisation. Family exist to consult, so an IMCA is not mandatory (s37), although advocacy may help. If disagreement persists despite second opinions, mediation or an ethics committee, the trust should apply to the Court of Protection. In an emergency, necessary treatment in her best interests may proceed.

questions.q: In the SPIKES protocol for breaking bad news, the 'K' stands for:
questions.why: K is 'Knowledge': giving information, preceded by a warning shot and delivered in small chunks without jargon.

questions.q: Distinguish the statutory duty of candour from the professional duty of candour. (4 marks)
markScheme: Statutory: Regulation 20, Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014
Applies to CQC-registered organisations for notifiable safety incidents: notify, apologise, provide information, follow up in writing
Professional: GMC/NMC duty on individual clinicians
Requires openness and honesty with patients when anything goes wrong, apology, explanation, and openness with colleagues/organisation (reporting)
questions.modelAnswer: The statutory duty of candour is in Regulation 20 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014 and is enforced by the CQC. It falls on registered organisations. When a notifiable safety incident occurs, they must tell the person as soon as reasonably practicable, apologise, give an account and information, and follow up in writing. The professional duty, set out by the GMC and NMC, falls on every individual clinician. They must be open and honest with patients whenever something goes wrong with their care, causing or potentially causing harm, apologise and explain. They must also report incidents and be honest with colleagues, employers and regulators.

questions.q: You are an FY1 on a surgical firm. Before a list, you notice the registrar smells strongly of alcohol and is unsteady. Outline the steps you should take. (4 marks)
markScheme: Patient safety first: act immediately, do not allow them to operate/treat patients
Speak to colleague if safe and appropriate, suggest they stop
Escalate promptly to consultant/clinical supervisor (or most senior available); GMC duty to raise concerns
Document, follow local policy; support colleague's health (occupational health); further escalation to medical director/GMC if unresolved
questions.modelAnswer: Patient safety takes priority (Good Medical Practice 2024). I would act immediately rather than wait. If safe, I would speak privately to the registrar, express concern and suggest they should not operate. Regardless of the response, I would escalate at once to the consultant in charge, or the most senior clinician available, so that the list is paused or covered. Seniority is no reason to stay silent. I would make a factual record and follow the trust's raising concerns policy. The colleague may have a health problem, so I would expect referral to occupational health and support. If the concern were not addressed, I would escalate to the clinical or medical director and, if needed, the GMC.

questions.q: Mrs Priya Nair, 58, attends clinic with her husband for the results of a CT scan arranged after weight loss. The scan shows a pancreatic mass with liver lesions, highly suggestive of metastatic cancer. She speaks fluent English; her husband is quiet and anxious. Describe how you would structure this consultation to break the news, explaining the reasoning behind each step. (12 marks)
markScheme: Preparation: read notes, confirm results, private room, no interruptions (bleep handed over), specialist nurse present, tissues
Perception: ask what she understands about why scan was done
Invitation: establish how much information she wants and whether husband should stay
Warning shot (e.g. 'I'm afraid the results are not what we hoped')
Knowledge: clear, jargon-free information in small chunks; use the word 'cancer'; pause
Emotions: allow silence, acknowledge and respond empathically (name, validate)
Check understanding (teach-back) and address ICE
Avoid false reassurance or premature prognosis figures; honest about uncertainty pending biopsy/MDT
Strategy: next steps (biopsy, MDT, oncology), symptom control, support, key worker contact
Summary, written information, follow-up arrangement
Document consultation and inform GP
questions.modelAnswer:
I would use the SPIKES framework (Baile and colleagues, 2000), adapted to Mrs Nair.

Setting. I would review the scan report and notes first so that I can answer questions accurately. I would book a private room, hand over my bleep, allow enough time and invite a clinical nurse specialist, who can become her key worker. Sitting at eye level with tissues available signals respect and attention.

Perception. I would ask what she understands about why the scan was done, for example 'What have you been told so far?' This shows me her starting point and any misunderstandings, so I can pitch information correctly.

Invitation. I would check how much detail she wants and confirm she is happy for her husband to stay. People differ in how they want information, and respecting that supports autonomy.

Knowledge. I would give a warning shot ('I'm afraid the scan has shown something serious'), pause, then explain in plain words that there is a growth in the pancreas that looks like cancer and that it appears to have spread to the liver. I would use the word 'cancer' so there is no ambiguity, and give information in small chunks.

Emotions. I would allow silence and respond empathically to the reactions of both Mrs and Mr Nair, naming and validating emotions ('This is a lot to take in'). Information is not absorbed while distress is unaddressed.

Strategy and summary. When they are ready, I would explore their ideas, concerns and expectations, and be honest about uncertainty. A biopsy and multidisciplinary team discussion are needed before treatment options and prognosis can be clarified, so I would avoid premature figures but not give false reassurance. I would outline next steps (tissue diagnosis, MDT, oncology review), symptom control, and practical and psychological support. I would check understanding with teach-back, give written information and the key worker's contact details, and arrange early follow-up.

Finally, I would document the conversation and inform her GP so that her care stays consistent.

questions.q: Dr Tom Ellis, an FY1, prescribes a penicillin-class antibiotic to Mr Brian Shah, 70, on a busy night shift, missing a documented penicillin allergy. Mr Shah develops a rash and wheeze after the first dose; he is treated promptly and recovers fully. The next morning, a nurse suggests 'there's no need to make a fuss as he's fine'. Discuss Dr Ellis's professional and legal obligations and how the incident should be handled by him and by the trust. (16 marks)
markScheme: Immediate clinical priority: treatment of anaphylaxis/allergic reaction, senior review, documentation of reaction and allergy status
Professional duty of candour (GMC/NMC): tell patient, apologise, explain what happened and consequences
Statutory duty of candour (reg 20) applies to trust if harm meets threshold of notifiable safety incident; trust to notify/apologise in writing
Apology is not admission of liability (Compensation Act 2006 s2)
Report incident through local system (e.g. LFPSE) and inform supervisor; 'no fuss' suggestion rejected
Good Medical Practice 2024: honesty, patient safety, learning, colleagues and culture
Reflection and learning (e-portfolio), with GMC position on reflective notes; focus on systems
Systems analysis: allergy recording, electronic prescribing alerts, workload, fatigue, pharmacist checks; just culture
Patient Safety Incident Response Framework approach: learning, not blame
Legal: negligence elements (duty, breach, causation, damage); minor harm, claim possible but not proof of misconduct
Fitness to practise unlikely for honest, isolated error; concealment would be serious misconduct
Support for doctor's wellbeing
questions.modelAnswer:
Clinical priorities come first. Mr Shah's reaction must be treated according to the anaphylaxis algorithm with senior help. The drug must be stopped and the reaction recorded, and the allergy coded so it is visible on every system.

Candour. Good Medical Practice (2024) and the GMC/NMC openness guidance impose a professional duty of candour on Dr Ellis. He should tell Mr Shah what happened, apologise sincerely, explain the consequences and describe the steps to prevent recurrence. The nurse's suggestion must be rejected, because concealment is far graver than the error. An apology is not an admission of liability (s2 Compensation Act 2006). Separately, the trust has a statutory duty under Regulation 20 of the 2014 Regulations. If the incident is a notifiable safety incident (moderate harm or worse, which may include a reaction needing treatment), the trust must inform Mr Shah, apologise and follow up in writing.

Reporting. Dr Ellis should inform his consultant and report through the trust's incident system (in England, linked to Learn from Patient Safety Events) so the organisation can learn.

Systems. Under the Patient Safety Incident Response Framework, the trust should examine contributory factors rather than blame. Was the allergy visible? Did electronic prescribing alert? What were the night-shift workload and fatigue, and was a pharmacist check available? A just culture separates honest error from recklessness.

Reflection. Dr Ellis should reflect on his learning in his portfolio. The GMC has said it will not ask for reflective notes in fitness to practise investigations.

Legal exposure. Negligence requires duty, breach, causation and damage. A claim is possible, but damages would be small after full recovery. An isolated, honestly disclosed error is very unlikely to raise fitness-to-practise concerns, whereas dishonesty would.

Support. Being involved in an error is distressing. His educational supervisor should know, so that his wellbeing and training needs are addressed.
